title: Problems in Agriculture: What Filipino Farmers Face and What Helps
metaTitle: Problems in Agriculture in the Philippines and What Helps
metaDescription: The main problems in agriculture in the Philippines, from typhoons and late pests to debt and low farmgate prices, and what a farmer can do about each.
keywords: problems in agriculture in the Philippines
excerpt: The biggest problems in agriculture in the Philippines are typhoons and dry spells, pests caught too late, costly inputs and debt, low farmgate prices, small farms, aging farmers and too little technical advice. No single fix covers them all. Still, each one has steps a farmer can take this season, and this guide lists them.

blocks.text:
Most agricultural problems feed each other. A typhoon flattens the crop, so the farmer borrows to replant. Then the loan pushes a quick sale at harvest, when the price is lowest.

So the goal is not to fix everything at once. It is to find the problem that cost you the most last season, and to work on that one first.
What are the main problems in agriculture in the Philippines?

blocks.text: Typhoons, floods and dry spells

About 20 tropical cyclones enter Philippine waters in an average year, and several cross the farm belts of Luzon and the Visayas. In La Nina years, rain and floods come more often. Then an El Nino year brings the opposite: late rains, short wet seasons and dry canals.

You cannot stop the weather, but you can plan around it. Plant so the crop flowers and ripens outside your worst storm weeks. Keep drains and canals clean before the rainy months. When a storm is coming and the grain is mature enough, harvest early instead of waiting for the full count. Our [typhoon preparation guide](/blog/typhoon-preparation-for-farmers) lists the steps, and the [El Nino farming tips](/blog/el-nino-la-nina-farming-tips) cover the dry years.
Pests and diseases caught too late

Rice black bug, brown planthopper, stem borers, tungro and, in corn, the fall armyworm all start small. Most farmers notice them only when whole patches turn yellow or brown. By then, a spray costs more and saves less.

The fix is cheap but takes habit. Walk each lot once a week, part the plants and look at the base, the leaves and the undersides. Learn the two or three pests that hit your crop at each stage. If you do spray, use a product registered for that pest and crop, and follow the label and the FPA registration. Our guide to [integrated pest management](/pests/integrated-pest-management) shows how to decide when a spray is worth it.
Input costs, debt and low farmgate prices
Costs and debt

Fertilizer, seed, fuel and labor take most of a season's money, and many farmers borrow for them. Some loans come from the five six lender, where you borrow five and pay back six. Others come from a trader who lends the inputs and then buys the harvest at his own price.

Cutting waste is the surest saving. A soil test tells you which nutrients the field already has, so you stop buying what it does not need. Our guide on how to [lower fertilizer cost](/blog/lower-fertilizer-cost) explains the usual savings. Also write down every expense, because you cannot cut a cost you never counted.
Prices and middlemen

At harvest, everyone sells at once, and wet palay goes for less than dry. Traders hold the most power in those weeks. Farmers who can dry their grain, store it safely or sell together through a cooperative often get a better price. Besides, a farmer who knows his own cost per kilo knows the lowest price he can accept. See the [cost of producing rice per hectare](/blog/cost-of-producing-rice-per-hectare) for a worked example.
Small farms, aging farmers and scarce labor

Many Filipino farms are only a hectare or two, and each generation splits them further among heirs. Small fields make a tractor, a combine or a truckload of fertilizer cost more per hectare. Meanwhile, many young people leave for the city, and the farmers who stay are getting older. At transplanting and harvest, crews are hard to find.

Working with neighbors helps here. Planting at the same time lets a group hire one machine for many small lots, and it keeps pests from moving from field to field. For the hardest jobs, hire a service provider for the transplanter or the combine harvester. Our page on [agricultural technology](/blog/agricultural-technology) compares the machines a small farm can rent.
Poor records and little technical advice

Ask a farmer which of his lots made money last season, and many cannot say. Without records, the same mistakes repeat. A notebook works, as long as every cost, every bag and every sale goes in it. Our guide to [farm record keeping](/blog/farm-record-keeping) shows what to write down.

Advice is the other gap. A town may have one or two agricultural technicians for thousands of farmers, so many decisions rest on a neighbor's guess or a store clerk's tip. A good answer needs three things: what you see, the crop's age, and the weather lately.

blocks.text: Questions about problems in agriculture

items.q: What is the biggest problem in agriculture in the Philippines?
items.a: For most farmers it is risk with little cushion: typhoons, floods and dry spells hit farms that already earn thin margins. Low farmgate prices and costly inputs make each loss harder to recover from.

items.q: What are the problems of agriculture a farmer can control?
items.a: Timing, pest scouting, fertilizer rates, records and how you sell. You cannot control the weather or the market, but you can plant in a safer window, catch pests early, stop wasting fertilizer and know your cost per kilo.

items.q: How can technology help with problems in farming?
items.a: Machines ease the labor shortage, and phone tools help with timing and advice. In anee.io, Anee, the smart farm technician, reads a photo of a pest with your lot's crop, stage and weather, and the calendar dates every task. She comes with Libre plus Anee at PHP 100 a month, and her answers use credits.

items.q: Is farming in the Philippines still worth it?
items.a: It can be, but margins are thin, so the farms that do well watch their costs and timing closely. Our page on [farm profitability](/blog/farm-profitability) shows where the money goes.
